name: Marco Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead percussion for a small touring theatre troupe, write rhythm charts and teach four weekend drummers. I have a music master’s and can steady a difficult ensemble; the troupe is a nonprofit that pays a low flat fee and long travel eats it further. I love a clean cue under an actor’s last word, but loading drums after midnight hurts more than it used to.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner cooks at the hospital, and our children are grown. The mortgage is still there and we have about two weeks of expenses saved; only a few comparable music posts exist nearby. I use AI now and then to sort my own set lists, but I check them against the stage manager’s marked score.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the troupe that faster set lists are fine if the travel and rehearsal fees stay on the call sheet. I would ask the manager to sign each tour date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks saved is barely a missed van hire, and our flat touring fee is low after travel. The plateau leaves the work in place, but I still worry about the mortgage when a show pays late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the paid tour and four pupils, request signed dates and travel reimbursement, and ask for my actual pension estimate. In the first plateau year I would compare the estimate with the mortgage and save a tenth of any cleared extra teaching fee after bills toward one month of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about ordinary cash flow, not excited by a quicker list. A drummer can play a full house and still come home short after the van bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is missing from the tour sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The exact mileage, van share and rehearsal time. I would match them with the signed agreement before I load a drum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the pension estimate end touring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know the figure yet. My partner and I would compare it with our bills before naming a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the troupe that software may write rhythm charts, but a paid drummer still reads an actor’s breath. I would ask which chart and live rehearsal fees remain in the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Charts bring about a quarter of my own pay, and I expect the troupe to commission fewer. With only two weeks saved, a cheaper chart can become a missed mortgage payment even while I am still on stage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would get written chart and tour rates and ask for a paid lesson on a new rhythm-checking tool, which is different from my occasional AI set lists. In disruption’s first year I would test only my own nameless demo after the troupe approves local storage, compare every cue by ear and against the marked score, and stop if timing changes or a file leaves the venue; I would keep the paid tour and pupils while checking actual fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing some chart pay on top of a thin cushion. A tidy machine chart cannot pay a tour invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you upload an actor’s rehearsal?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would use only a demo I made without names or another player’s part. The troupe must approve local storage first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the lesson is unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current score checks and wait for paid instruction. The troupe cannot turn a paid rehearsal into free software training.

A **two-week reserve** leaves little room for the loss.

fieldNote: The **new AI learning** is a rhythm checker, beyond his occasional set-list use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the troupe that thinking AGI by 2028 could make charts and bookings before robot drummers arrive around 2031. I would request signed live tour dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect chart commissions to stop and some tour preparation pay to fall in 2028, taking more than a quarter of my income. Two weeks saved and few nearby posts make the replacement search urgent, even if live playing lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would total chart invoices and keep signed tour and pupil hours. In the first year after 2028, if charts end and paid preparation falls, I would apply for a posted paid community percussion leader role only if my music master’s and ensemble-leading years meet its requirements, actual live teaching and preparation are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces the loss with a workable last bus; I would retain current work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about a large fast cut to my own pay. I can compare a real community post, but I cannot count one that has not been advertised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the date matter before robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI can price a rhythm chart in 2028. A robot drummer on the stage comes about three years later, around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a volunteer music leader title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would read the paid live hours and net after travel. The title alone will not pay our mortgage.

do: Keep **tour and pupils** with signed hours before 2028.
Seek **posted percussion leader** after chart/prep loss; require accepted master’s/leadership and paid live teaching/preparation.
Require **written replacement net** after travel and last bus; retain current work until signed offer.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about a large likely pay cut.
S2.quote: I can compare a real community post, but I cannot count one that has not been advertised.
fieldNote: The **2028 loss** reaches chart thinking and preparation before robot drumming around 2031.
A **posted paid role** must accept his master’s and leadership and replace lost net pay after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stage crew that five years until thinking AGI around 2031 gives us time to find paid sound work. Robot drummers around 2034 arrive after the chart work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect charts to thin, and the touring van is harder on my back each year. I have handled cables but am not qualified to run a sound desk; an unpaid course would eat the two weeks of money we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would ask a venue about a posted paid sound-assistant role and enrol in a live-sound certificate only after it confirms an actual funded place with paid training hours, no lost tour or pupil wages, a last bus, and written recognition of the certificate for that posting before enrolment. In the first year after 2031, if chart or tour fees fall, I would apply for that posted paid sound-assistant role only after completing the accepted certificate. I would move only on a signed written net offer after travel that replaces lost pay and a workable last bus; until then I would keep the tour and pupils, then start technician-supervised checks and avoid solo crowded shows before signed equipment and safety clearance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the chart money over five years, but a funded paid place would let me test another skill. A sound certificate is a key to an application, not a wage in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you run the desk alone after class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A venue technician would supervise my first checks. I would wait for signed equipment and safety clearance before a crowded show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only tuition is free?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the tour and pupils. Paid training hours and current wages must survive, or I cannot enrol.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell fellow players that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot drummers around 2039 are different clocks. I would ask for today’s rehearsal and travel rates in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want fewer midnight loads, but I have not seen a pension estimate. Our flat low fee and two-week reserve make present bills uncertain, even with a decade before the chart market changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid tour and pupils, request my actual pension estimate and signed travel rates, and save a tenth of any cleared extra teaching fee after mortgage, food and travel toward one month of bills. Across the decade I would compare the actual pension estimate and health with tour pay; in the first year after 2036 I would take only paid dates that cover travel and keep the pupils while hours remain, rather than treat a future robot date as a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the present mortgage and tour costs. A decade of notice does not add a week to our savings today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date at 68?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I need the actual pension amount, bills and health in front of us. I would not decide from a birthday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no extra teaching fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I save nothing extra from teaching that month. One month of bills is a target, not a balance I already have.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because charts and preparation could lose over a quarter of my pay before I find another post. Signed tour hours, a real paid percussion role and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many hours it takes to load a drum kit after the audience has gone. A flat fee can shrink on the drive home, even when the stage sounded full.

headlineQuote: A flat fee can shrink on the drive home, even when the stage sounded full.
portrait: Marco is a **senior percussion leader** with a music master’s and excellent ensemble skill at a low-paid nonprofit troupe.
He has **two weeks saved**, a hospital-cook partner, grown children and a mortgage.
He uses **AI occasionally** for set lists and would learn a new checker only with paid instruction and manual verification.
He considers **funded sound training** with protected current wages, a recognised certificate and supervised first checks.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** could remove chart and preparation income worth over a quarter of his pay.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed tour hours**, a posted paid percussion role and written replacement net after travel.
